claims.text: What the image looks like Bowel wall thickening, pneumatosis intestinalis, portal venous gas → bowel ischemia
claims.quote: Bowel wall thickening, pneumatosis intestinalis, portal venous gas Bowel ischemia

claims.text: Example CT angiogram: the superior mesenteric artery shows an abrupt cutoff of IV contrast, with some small bowel thickening (embolism from the heart in a patient with atrial fibrillation)
claims.quote: In this image, the arrow points to the superior mesenteric artery, which has an abrupt cutoff of IV contrast. Some thickening of the small bowel in the left abdomen is seen. This case of embolism is from the heart in a patient with atrial fibrillation.

claims.text: Aspects (abnormal in red) Plain radiographs mainly rule out other causes (eg, perforated viscus); portal venous gas or pneumatosis intestinalis may be seen late; these also appear on CT, which may directly show vascular occlusion (more accurately on the venous side)
claims.quote: Plain abdominal radiographs are useful mainly in ruling out other causes of pain (eg, perforated viscus), although portal venous gas or pneumatosis intestinalis may be seen late in the disease. These findings also appear on CT, which may also directly visualize vascular occlusion—more accurately on the venous side.

claims.text: Other imaging and serum markers lack sensitivity and specificity early, when diagnosis is most critical
claims.quote: Other imaging studies and serum markers can show abnormalities but lack sensitivity and specificity early in the course of the disease when diagnosis is most critical.

claims.text: Clear peritoneal signs → straight to the OR; otherwise selective mesenteric angiography or CT angiography is the diagnostic procedure of choice
claims.quote: Patients with clear peritoneal signs should proceed directly to the operating room for both diagnosis and treatment. For others, selective mesenteric angiography or CT angiography is the diagnostic procedure of choice.

claims.text: Serum markers (eg, creatine kinase, lactate) rise with necrosis but are nonspecific and seen later
claims.quote: Serum markers (eg, creatine kinase, lactate) rise with necrosis but are nonspecific findings that are seen later.

claims.text: Causes Interruption of intestinal blood flow by embolism, thrombosis, or a low-flow state
claims.quote: Acute mesenteric ischemia is interruption of intestinal blood flow by embolism, thrombosis, or a low-flow state.

claims.text: Arterial embolus (> 40%): CAD, heart failure, valvular disease, atrial fibrillation, prior emboli; arterial thrombosis (30%): generalized atherosclerosis
claims.quote: Arterial embolus (> 40%) | Coronary artery disease, heart failure, valvular heart disease, atrial fibrillation, history of arterial emboli | Arterial thrombosis (30%) | Generalized atherosclerosis
claims.locator: Causes of Acute Mesenteric Ischemia table

claims.text: Venous thrombosis (15%): hypercoagulable states, inflammatory conditions, trauma, heart failure, renal failure, portal hypertension; nonocclusive (15%): low-flow states, splanchnic vasoconstriction (eg, vasopressors, cocaine)
claims.quote: Venous thrombosis (15%) | Hypercoagulable states, inflammatory conditions (eg, pancreatitis, diverticulitis), trauma, heart failure, renal failure, portal hypertension, decompression sickness | Nonocclusive ischemia (15%) | Low-flow states (eg, heart failure, shock, cardiopulmonary bypass), splanchnic vasoconstriction (eg, vasopressors, cocaine)

claims.text: Necrosis can occur as soon as 6 hours after symptom onset
claims.quote: Necrosis can occur as soon as 6 hours after the onset of symptoms.

claims.text: Symptoms Early hallmark: severe pain but minimal physical findings (soft abdomen, little or no tenderness); later, peritonitis, possibly heme-positive stool, and shock
claims.quote: The early hallmark of mesenteric ischemia is severe pain but minimal physical findings. The abdomen remains soft, with little or no tenderness. Mild tachycardia may be present. Later, as necrosis develops, signs of peritonitis appear, with marked abdominal tenderness, guarding, rigidity, and no bowel sounds. The stool may be heme-positive (increasingly likely as ischemia progresses). The usual signs of shock develop and are frequently followed by death.

claims.text: Sudden onset suggests (not diagnostic) arterial embolism; gradual onset is typical of venous thrombosis; prior postprandial pain (intestinal angina) suggests arterial thrombosis
claims.quote: Sudden onset of pain suggests but is not diagnostic of an arterial embolism, whereas a more gradual onset is typical of venous thrombosis. Patients with a history of postprandial abdominal discomfort (which suggests intestinal angina) may have arterial thrombosis.

claims.text: Treatment and next step Her chart: emergent laparotomy
Resuscitate with IV fluids and start broad-spectrum antibiotics
claims.quote: Patients should be resuscitated with intravenous fluids to improve visceral perfusion. Broad-spectrum antibiotics should be initiated.

claims.text: At laparotomy, options are embolectomy, revascularization or resection; a second-look laparotomy may be needed
claims.quote: If diagnosis is made during exploratory laparotomy, options are surgical embolectomy, revascularization, and resection. A second-look laparotomy may be needed to reassess the viability of questionable areas of bowel.

claims.text: Peritoneal signs at any time suggest the need for immediate surgery; mesenteric venous thrombosis without peritonitis can be treated with anticoagulants
claims.quote: The development of peritoneal signs at any time during the evaluation suggests the need for immediate surgery. Re-establishment of blood flow to the bowel can sometimes be accomplished through endovascular techniques. Mesenteric venous thrombosis without signs of peritonitis can be treated with anticoagulant medications.
